tasks.title: Define OS/system metric ingestion contract
tasks.problem: pgstat must distinguish PostgreSQL bottlenecks from host CPU, memory, disk, filesystem, and network bottlenecks without adding load to the target PostgreSQL database.
requirements: Define supported OS families and variants: Linux generic, RHEL/Rocky/Alma/CentOS/Fedora family, Ubuntu/Debian family, SUSE family, and Windows Server. Unsupported OS behavior must be explicit.
Define source adapters: optional read-only OS user collection, optional node_exporter/windows_exporter scrape/import, optional Telegraf/Prometheus bridge, and manual/API ingestion.
OS collection must not query or load the target PostgreSQL database. Only central pgstat storage may be written.
Direct OS collection must use least privilege. Default design should work with a read-only OS user and command/source allowlist; no root/sudo requirement by default.
Define host identity and OS change history so a machine can move from Windows to Linux, RHEL to Ubuntu, or similar without corrupting historical evidence.

Define PostgreSQL instance to host/container binding: automatic evidence-based matching, explicit manual override, binding confidence, ambiguity handling, valid_from/valid_to history, and no AI high-confidence use when binding is missing or low-confidence.

Define host service health observation for PostgreSQL-related services: PostgreSQL server, PgBouncer, Patroni, pgpool-II, HAProxy/Keepalived when tagged as PostgreSQL traffic components, and container/Kubernetes equivalents.

Define a fast service heartbeat separate from heavier OS metric cadence so stopped, failed, unhealthy, or restart-looping PostgreSQL-related services can alert quickly without querying the target PostgreSQL database.

Define minimum metrics: CPU/load/iowait/steal, memory/swap, disk IOPS/throughput/latency/utilization, filesystem bytes/inodes, network throughput/errors/drops, and optional PostgreSQL process CPU/memory where safely available.
Define missing/stale/partial coverage behavior. Missing OS metrics must never be silently treated as zero or healthy evidence.
Define schedule, retention, purge, partition, rollup, units, security, export, and AI evidence policy.

acceptance_criteria.text: Supported OS families, unsupported OS behavior, and OS change history model are documented.
Collection source adapters are documented with target DB load impact explicitly stated as zero.
Read-only OS user / least-privilege model is documented for direct collection.
Instance-host/container binding model is documented with automatic evidence sources, manual override, confidence levels, ambiguity behavior, and historical validity ranges.

PostgreSQL-related service health contract is documented, including service discovery sources, allowlist/tag model, status values, fast heartbeat cadence, alert transitions, and container/Kubernetes service health mapping.
Minimum metric list includes units, cadence, retention, purge, partition, and rollup decisions.
Missing/stale/partial metrics behavior is documented and blocks high-confidence findings when needed.
pgdbaagent optional evidence usage is documented without making OS metrics silently mandatory.

tasks.title: Raise a system alert when a ready instance loses pg_hba access, readable in Telegram and UI
tasks.problem: Customer-reported bug (2026-07-17), root-caused via systematic debugging: when a previously working instance loses its pg_hba.conf entry (or otherwise fails auth/connect), JobOrchestrator.processClusterInstance/processStatementsInstance catch the exception, call stateRepo.updateAfterFailure (consecutive_failures++), then call handleSecretOrAuthError which matches the message on 'connect'/'authentication'/'password'/'secret_ref' and calls inventoryRepo.scheduleBootstrapRetry — this flips instance_inventory.bootstrap_state to 'degraded'. findDueInstances only selects bootstrap_state='ready' (InventoryRepository.java:155), so the instance drops out of the collection queue on the very next cycle and consecutive_failures freezes (usually at 1). SystemHealthEvaluator.checkInstanceUnreachable only opens SYSTEM_INSTANCE_UNREACHABLE when consecutive_failures >= 3 (SystemHealthEvaluator.java:195), so the threshold is never reached. BootstrapHandler then silently retries the degraded instance on a backoff schedule (1min/5min/15min/1hour) with no alert at any point. Net effect: an instance could sit unmonitored indefinitely with zero Telegram/system alert, only an INFO log line ('Instance degraded'a cekildi'). Follow-up (2026-07-27): once the alert did fire, the customer reported it was uninterpretable in Telegram ('Instance unreachable ... The connection attempt failed.' with no host name anywhere) and the UI's InstanceDetail degraded-reason banner didn't recognize this alert code either.

Keep the fix minimal: no new alert code, no new migration — reuse existing AlertService/AlertCode/notification plumbing and the existing BootstrapBanner UI component.

tasks.title: Stop AlertService.upsertSystemAlert from reopening and re-notifying acknowledged alerts
tasks.problem: Customer reported (2026-07-27) that acknowledging a 'Stat collection failed' alert (STAT_COLLECTION_FAILED) did not stop it from repeating in Telegram. Root cause: AlertService.upsertSystemAlert unconditionally set status='open' and acknowledged_at=null on every upsert (AlertRepository had the same pattern in upsert/upsertAdaptive/upsertAdaptiveWithSeverity), and shouldNotifySystemOpen() treats any non-'open' previousStatus (including 'acknowledged') as a reason to notify. So the moment an acknowledged alert's underlying condition re-triggered (e.g. the same collector job failing again 5 minutes later), the alert silently flipped back to 'open' and re-notified — acknowledge provided no suppression at all, contrary to customer expectation. Discussion clarified the desired behavior: acknowledge should NOT suppress notifications; the customer wants the alert to keep repeating at its normal cadence until they explicitly resolve it — but the current code's problem was that 'acknowledged' status was being silently and incorrectly reset to 'open' with acknowledged_at wiped, which is misleading in the UI even though notifications kept flowing.
requirements: An acknowledged alert whose condition keeps re-triggering must keep notifying at the normal cadence (existing NotificationService cooldown logic already throttles repeat sends) — acknowledge is a note, not a mute.

An acknowledged alert's status must stay 'acknowledged' (not silently flip back to 'open') while the underlying condition is still active, so the UI accurately reflects that someone already looked at it.
A 'resolved' alert reopening (genuinely new occurrence) must still flip to 'open' and notify as before — only the 'acknowledged' case changes.
Only the user's explicit resolve action (or the code's own resolveSystemAlert call once the root cause clears) should end the repeat cycle.

A 'resolved' alert reopening on re-trigger is unaffected (still flips to 'open' and notifies as before).

Adjust the post-upsert notify decision: when previousStatus was 'acknowledged', notify whenever severity is warning/critical (same threshold as new alerts), instead of relying on shouldNotifySystemOpen's open/severity-escalation logic which assumed status was always 'open' or terminal.
Scope limited to upsertSystemAlert (the system-alert path used by SystemHealthEvaluator/JobOrchestrator/BootstrapHandler); AlertRepository's adaptive-rule upsert paths were not touched in this pass.

tasks.title: Fix agg.pg_table_stat_hourly rollup ON CONFLICT crash on renamed/OID-reused tables
tasks.problem: Customer-reported (2026-08-17) after the P0-026 upgrade: collector logs showed 'Rollup job hatasi: ... bad SQL grammar [insert into agg.pg_table_stat_hourly ...] Caused by: ERROR: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time'. Root cause: AggRepository.rollupTableStatHourly()'s GROUP BY included schemaname/relname in addition to the ON CONFLICT target (bucket_start, instance_pk, dbid, relid). If the same relid appears with two different schemaname/relname values within the same hourly window (table renamed, or OID reused after a drop+create), the GROUP BY produces two rows that the ON CONFLICT target treats as one, and PostgreSQL rejects the double-affect. rollupHourly() (pgss) does not have this bug because its GROUP BY already matches its ON CONFLICT target exactly.
requirements: GROUP BY must match the ON CONFLICT target exactly so a single relid never produces more than one row per hourly window.

schemaname/relname must still reflect a real observed value (not dropped) — use the same 'last observed in window' pattern already used for n_live_tup_last/n_dead_tup_last/n_mod_since_analyze_last in the same query.
No new migration, no new alert code — pure SQL fix inside the existing rollup method.

tasks.title: TextEnricher's pg_stat_statements(true) call materializes the whole view, spilling to temp files
tasks.problem: Customer reported (2026-08-21) recurring temp file WARN log lines on two monitored source instances, e.g. 'temporary file: path base/pgsql_tmp/pgsql_tmp1951006.1, size 9526206' appearing every ~1 minute from user=pgstats_collector. Raising work_mem 2MB->4MB on the target instance only shrank, not eliminated, the temp files, ruling out work_mem sizing as the real fix. Live pg_stat_statements query on the target instance identified the exact two collector-issued statements responsible: the pgssStatsQuery-style CTE around pg_stat_statements($1) (~10MB temp/call) and 'select queryid, query from pg_stat_statements($1)' (~3MB temp/call) — both from TextEnricher.enrich(). Root cause: TextEnricher.pgssTextQuery() called pg_stat_statements(true) with no WHERE clause at all, so PostgreSQL materializes the query-text column (often the largest part of the view) for every actively tracked statement on the instance, not just the handful of queryids TextEnricher actually needs (the pendingSeries batch, size = batchSize). On instances with many/long tracked statements this exceeds work_mem and spills to disk every enrichment cycle. Also relevant: the target instance was PG12 at initial diagnosis and has since been upgraded to PG17 mid-investigation; the fix must apply to every PG version family since pgssTextQuery has no per-version override.
requirements: TextEnricher must only ask the source instance for the specific queryids it needs to enrich in this batch, not the entire pg_stat_statements view.

Fix must apply uniformly across all supported PG major versions (11-18) — pgssTextQuery is defined once in Pg11_12Queries and inherited by Pg13/Pg14_16/Pg17_18, so a single change covers all of them, confirmed no subclass overrides it.
No new alert code or migration needed — this is a pure query-shape fix in the collector.

acceptance_criteria.text: Pg11_12Queries.pgssTextQuery() adds 'where queryid = any(?)' to the pg_stat_statements(true) call.
TextEnricher.enrich() switches from Statement to PreparedStatement and binds the pending queryids (queryIdToSeriesId.keySet()) as a bigint array parameter.
mvn compile && mvn test pass with the new PreparedStatement/array-binding code.

Live verification: after deploying, the two source instances that were producing temp-file WARN log lines every ~1 minute stop producing them (or shrink dramatically, proportional to batchSize instead of total tracked statement count).

SourceConnectionFactory.configureSession() sets work_mem to 32MB on every ephemeral source-instance connection, addressing the separate/larger root cause found via fleet-wide analysis: pg_stat_statements(false)'s own set-returning-function materialization (used by StatementsCollector's per-cycle pgssStatsQuery(), not just TextEnricher) exceeds a small source-side work_mem on instances with thousands of tracked statements, independent of any WHERE filter (this query legitimately needs every tracked statement, so it can't be narrowed the way pgssTextQuery was).
mvn compile && mvn test pass with the work_mem session-level fix.

Live verification: fleet-wide query against fact.pgss_delta joined to dim.query_text confirms the highest-volume instances (etscore-dev-test-253.50, emh-dev-test-142.80, archdb-dev-142.49, moneasy-dev-147.50, moneasy-test-167.50, and others) stop accumulating temp_blks_written for both the pgssStatsQuery CTE and any lingering unfiltered pgssTextQuery calls.

implementation_plan: Pg11_12Queries.pgssTextQuery(): 'select queryid, query from %s(true) where queryid = any(?)'.

TextEnricher.enrich(): build Long[] pendingQueryIds from queryIdToSeriesId.keySet() (guaranteed non-empty since pendingSeries.isEmpty() already short-circuits earlier), switch the query execution to conn.prepareStatement(...) + stmt.setArray(1, conn.createArrayOf("bigint", pendingQueryIds)), keep the same row-processing loop inside the try-with-resources ResultSet block.

SourceConnectionFactory.configureSession(): add 'SET work_mem = ''32MB''' alongside the existing statement_timeout/lock_timeout SETs — applies to every ephemeral source connection (StatementsCollector, TextEnricher, and any other collector using SourceConnectionFactory.connect()), scoped to the connection's own session only, does not touch the source instance's persistent configuration.
verification_plan: Live: on the two originally affected source instances, watch postgres logs (log_temp_files is already on) for at least 10-15 minutes after deploy and confirm the pgstats_collector temp-file lines from TextEnricher's statement no longer appear (or are much smaller, bounded by batch size).

Live: fleet-wide, query fact.pgss_delta/dim.statement_series/dim.query_text on the central pgstat database for temp_blks_written_delta > 0 rows where query_text ilike '%pg_stat_statements%', across all instances, for several days post-deploy — confirm the volume trends toward zero for both the pgssStatsQuery CTE pattern and any unfiltered pgssTextQuery pattern.
verification_evidence: Customer shared postgres logs showing repeating temp_file WARN lines (9.5MB and 3.1MB, roughly every minute) from user=pgstats_collector on a source instance; raising work_mem 2MB->4MB reduced but did not eliminate them.

Customer ran pg_stat_statements on the target instance and shared the top temp_blks_written statements: the largest non-VACUUM entries were the collector's own pg_stat_statements($1)-wrapping CTE (~10MB/call, 11 calls) and 'select queryid, query from pg_stat_statements($1)' (~3MB/call, 11 calls) — both traced to TextEnricher.enrich() via Pg11_12Queries.pgssTextQuery().

Root cause confirmed by code read: pgssTextQuery() had no WHERE clause, so pg_stat_statements(true) materializes query text for every actively tracked statement on the instance, not just the queryids TextEnricher's current batch needs.

Fix applied: pgssTextQuery() now takes 'where queryid = any(?)'; TextEnricher switched from Statement to PreparedStatement with a bigint array bind of the pending queryids. mvn compile and mvn test pass with no regressions.

Second root cause found after deploy (2026-08-21): customer reported temp files still appearing ~14 minutes after deploying commit 6f92a78. docker inspect showed the collector image's Created timestamp was recent (matching the deploy), but the running jar was still executing the old unfiltered query — a Docker build-layer cache inconsistency (the COPY layer hash did not invalidate even though the compiled jar content changed). Customer ran `docker compose build --no-cache collector && docker compose up -d --force-recreate collector` manually on the server and confirmed temp files stopped appearing in the logs.

Preventive fix applied to ./pgstat's upgrade command: the UI-only --no-cache rebuild was extended to also force --no-cache for the collector service, so future deploys can't silently keep a stale jar behind a fresh-looking image. api is not yet covered by this protection (same risk theoretically possible, not reported so far) — flagged for follow-up if a similar symptom recurs there.

Third, larger root cause found via fleet-wide analysis (2026-08-21, after re-checking a specific source instance that still showed 9.5MB temp files post-deploy): querying fact.pgss_delta centrally across all monitored instances for query_text ilike '%pg_stat_statements%' with temp_blks_written_delta > 0 revealed the dominant temp-file producer was NOT TextEnricher's pgssTextQuery at all, but StatementsCollector's per-cycle pgssStatsQuery() CTE (the one wrapping pg_stat_statements(false), used for stats collection, no query text) — accounting for 20-24MB of accumulated temp per high-traffic instance over 3 days on 5+ instances (etscore-dev-test-253.50, emh-dev-test-142.80, archdb-dev-142.49, moneasy-dev-147.50, moneasy-test-167.50, and others), dwarfing the original TextEnricher issue. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the highest-volume instance confirmed the temp write originates in the pg_stat_statements(false) Function Scan itself (4758 rows, before to_jsonb/CTE even runs) — this query cannot be narrowed with a WHERE filter since it legitimately needs every tracked statement's stats every cycle, unlike pgssTextQuery. Also separately confirmed (unrelated false alarm during this same investigation): a handful of unfiltered pgssTextQuery calls (old query shape) were still showing up fleet-wide with recent timestamps in the same result set, alongside the new filtered shape — worth continued monitoring but not the dominant contributor.

Fix applied for the pgssStatsQuery/SRF-materialization cause: SourceConnectionFactory.configureSession() now also sets work_mem='32MB' on every ephemeral source connection (alongside the existing statement_timeout/lock_timeout SETs), scoped to the collector's own session only. mvn compile and mvn test pass.

Deployed to production 2026-08-21 ~16:07 +03 (collector container restart confirmed via docker inspect State.StartedAt=2026-08-21T13:07:22Z / 16:07:22+03; jar content confirmed via grep -a on the extracted class file inside the running container, 'SET work_mem = ''%dMB''' literal present). First fleet-wide check right after restart (window 16:08+) showed zero temp_blks_written from any collector-issued pg_stat_statements query (only the diagnostic 'select count(*) from pg_stat_statements' the user ran manually appeared). Second fleet-wide check ~1 hour later, filtered strictly to sample_ts > restart time (16:07:22+03), confirmed the same: zero rows from collector's own pgssStatsQuery or pgssTextQuery across all monitored instances, including the five previously highest-volume ones (etscore-dev-test-253.50, emh-dev-test-142.80, archdb-dev-142.49, moneasy-dev-147.50, moneasy-test-167.50). The only matching row was again the user's own manual diagnostic query. Fix confirmed durable across a ~1 hour post-restart window.

tasks.title: dead_tuple_ratio alert rule redesigned with a 3-signal bloat/vacuum-ineffectiveness model
tasks.problem: Customer reported (2026-08-21) that pgstat's own central database has ongoing autovacuum-vs-delete-rate imbalance (continuous DELETE workload, autovacuum not keeping up, dead tuple / wasted size growing) but no alert had ever fired. Investigation found dead_tuple_ratio alert rules existed but were disabled (is_enabled=false), and the underlying evaluation logic was a single-signal design: percentage-only, gated by a >1000 total-row minimum that silently excluded small-but-important tables (e.g. ops.alert at 592 rows with 22% dead tuples never qualified for evaluation at all). Customer explicitly asked for a more principled design that avoids false positives while still catching real bloat, and asked for a market-practice comparison (check_postgres, Datadog, pganalyze, Citus) before implementing.
requirements: Replace the single-threshold percentage model with a 3-signal model: (A) ratio + minimum-row-count gate (existing logic, threshold lowered/made configurable), (B) absolute dead-tuple-count threshold independent of row count (catches small-but-critical tables), (C) an autovacuum-ineffectiveness signal (N+ autovacuum runs in the window but dead tuples still not dropping).

All three thresholds must be optional/nullable per alert_rule row — if the customer leaves them blank, code-side best-practice defaults apply (bloat_min_rows=100, bloat_abs_dead_tup=500, bloat_vacuum_ineffective_count=20); if the customer fills them in, their values win.

UI must expose the three overrides only when metric_name is dead_tuple_ratio, following the existing 'optional override, blank = default' pattern already used for the adaptive rule's absolute-floor field.
Change must be backward compatible with existing table_metric evaluation for every other metric_name (no behavior change for non-dead_tuple_ratio rules).

acceptance_criteria.text: V089 migration adds bloat_min_rows, bloat_abs_dead_tup, bloat_vacuum_ineffective_count as nullable columns with >=0-or-null check constraints on control.alert_rule.

AlertRuleEvaluator gains a findBloatedTables() method implementing the 3-signal OR logic (ratio+min-rows) OR (absolute dead-tuple count), annotated with a vacuum_ineffective flag when the autovacuum-count signal fires; table_metric/dead_tuple_ratio routes to it instead of the generic table_metric query.
AlertRules.tsx exposes the three optional overrides (with default-value placeholders and explanatory copy) when metric_name === 'dead_tuple_ratio', wired through form state and the save payload.
mvn compile && mvn test and npx tsc --noEmit both pass with the new code.

Live verification: after migrating and deploying, re-enabling dead_tuple_ratio rules on the central pgstat database produces a real alert for the previously-missed bloat (e.g. ops.alert or ops.notification_log) without flooding false positives on healthy tables.

findBloatedTables() reads n_dead_tup_estimate/n_live_tup_estimate from the most recent sample in the window (DISTINCT ON ... ORDER BY sample_ts DESC) instead of max() across the window, so a manual VACUUM/cleanup is reflected as soon as the next db_objects collection cycle (up to 30 minutes, per schedule_profile.db_objects_interval_seconds) samples the lowered dead-tuple count — max() previously kept showing the pre-cleanup peak until the whole window aged out, delaying auto-resolve by up to double the collection interval. autovacuum_count_sum still sums the full window (a count-of-runs signal, not a point-in-time one).
mvn compile && mvn test pass with the DISTINCT ON / window-function rewrite.

evaluateThresholdPerRecord's cooldown check no longer blocks auto-resolve: the isInCooldown check now only gates opening/re-raising a new alert, not the exceeding.isEmpty()/severity==null resolve paths — so a manually-fixed table (or any granular metric that recovers) resolves as soon as the evaluator sees the recovered value, even while the rule's cooldown_minutes window from the last alert is still active. This affects every metric_type routed through evaluateThresholdPerRecord (statement/table/index granular thresholds), not just dead_tuple_ratio.

Root cause: evaluateThresholdPerRecord's isInCooldown(...) check (control.alert_rule_last_eval.last_alert_at within cooldown_minutes, 60 here) was a blanket 'continue' at the top of the per-instance loop, skipping the resolve branches (exceeding.isEmpty() / severity==null) along with the raise-new-alert branch — so once an alert fired, no resolve could happen until the full 60-minute cooldown expired, regardless of whether the underlying problem was already fixed. tasks.problem: Customer asked a conceptual question after watching the bloat alert system work all day: 'pgstat's own DB has ongoing DELETE-driven bloat, why doesn't autovacuum ever recover the space, shouldn't autovacuum let new writes reuse dead tuple space?' Investigated with fact.pg_relation_size_snapshot (nightly-collected real table size, not just dead_tup ratio) and found agg.pg_table_stat_hourly_202608 grew from 1457MB to 2723MB over 14 days (~87%) while agg fact-table partitions grew for the expected reason (new daily data). Live query on fact.pg_table_stat_delta showed n_live_tup_estimate=7,062,216 constant while n_dead_tup_estimate climbed from 1,121,145 to 1,194,965 within a few hours — live count NOT changing, dead count climbing: a strong signal of repeated UPDATE, not INSERT growth. control.table_relopts_snapshot confirmed no per-table autovacuum_enabled override; last_autovacuum was ~9 hours old with autovacuum_count_delta=0 since. Root-caused via code read (Explore agent): AggRepository.rollupTableStatHourly()/rollupPgssHourly() UPSERT (on conflict on the full PK: bucket_start/instance_pk/dbid/relid or equivalent) the SAME current-hour bucket rows every ~5 minutes (JobOrchestrator's readHourlyRollupIntervalSec guard, default 300s) — roughly 12 real UPDATEs per row per hour, each leaving a dead tuple via MVCC. At this table's scale (~7M rows), the default autovacuum trigger (threshold=50 + scale_factor=0.2 × live_tup ≈ 1.4M dead tuples) takes far too long to reach relative to the actual update rate, so the table bloats for days before autovacuup ever fires — not a bug in the rollup logic (which is correct and necessary), but a mismatch between this table's write pattern (small delta, many updates) and Postgres's row-count-scaled default vacuum threshold.

Fix must be a per-table storage parameter (ALTER TABLE ... SET), not a change to the rollup logic itself — the UPSERT-every-5-minutes design is correct and intentional (JobOrchestrator already has a 5-minute guard to prevent worse, per-poll-cycle UPSERTs).
Must apply automatically to future monthly partitions of these two tables, not require a migration per partition.

The dead_tuple_ratio alert's top-candidate selection must surface this table when it IS the biggest problem — the customer separately asked 'neden pg stat bu bloatı yakalamadı, alertlerde görmedim hiç bu tabloları' (why didn't pgstat catch this bloat, I never saw these tables in the alerts) after this investigation, which surfaced a second, distinct bug (see AC3).

tasks.title: Add observational autovacuum-pressure evidence (I/O operation counts, wait-event distribution) to the existing bloat alert
tasks.problem: After PGSTAT-P1-010's fix (lowering autovacuum thresholds on two high-UPSERT hourly rollup tables) and PGSTAT-P0-036 AC7 (a new alert scenario that recommends lowering thresholds for chronically-updated tables), the customer asked a sharp follow-up: 'autovacuum'un etkisini de ölçmeliyiz, sık sık devreye girerek sistemi yavaşlatıyor da olabilir' (we should measure autovacuum's impact too — frequent triggering could be slowing the system down). The concern is real and well-documented (worker saturation, cost-based throttling misconfiguration), and pgstat currently has no instrumentation for it: fetchAutovacuumWorkerStatus() only counts running workers (and does so incorrectly, via count(*) instead of distinct pid), fact.pg_progress_vacuum_snapshot only has progress metrics, and fact.pg_io_stat_delta's backend_type column could isolate autovacuum-worker I/O but nothing aggregates it. This means every 'lower your autovacuum threshold' recommendation pgstat makes is one-sided — it addresses bloat with no counter-evidence about autovacuum pressure. SCOPE NOTE (revised after four review rounds): the achievable goal is OBSERVATIONAL evidence, not a causal cost measurement. PostgreSQL exposes no per-process CPU time, pg_stat_io is cluster-wide operation counts (not bytes, not disk IOPS, not per-table), and wait-event data is point-in-time sampling that cannot prove backlog or single-cause attribution. The task therefore adds carefully-worded observational evidence sentences to the existing dead_tuple_ratio alert — it does NOT deliver a causal 'autovacuum cost' metric, and the earlier framing of this task (title mentioning CPU, requirements asking for an 'X MB/s' chart) was not achievable as stated.
requirements: Add observational autovacuum-pressure evidence to the existing dead_tuple_ratio alert's diagnosis text (scenarios 3 and 4.5): autovacuum-worker I/O operation counts vs. client-backend counts where available (PG16+ only, via fact.pg_io_stat_delta backend_type + object='relation'), and the wait-event distribution of autovacuum-worker samples (IO wait / VacuumDelay throttle sleep / no-wait-event / other) from fact.pg_activity_snapshot.

All generated text must stay observational, never causal: report what was sampled ('worker observed in throttle sleep in N% of samples'), never assert a diagnosis ('throttling is slowing the table down') or a hardware conclusion ('the disk is slow'). Every signal must distinguish unsupported-version / unknown-capability / no-data / real-zero / available rather than collapsing them into one N/A.

A 'lower cost_delay' recommendation may only fire when the effective (table-override-aware, -1-fallback-resolved) cost_delay is strictly GREATER than the version default (20ms on PG11, 2ms on PG12+) AND the throttle-sleep evidence is statistically sufficient — never on a high IO-wait ratio alone, and never when the setting is at or below the version default.

OUT OF SCOPE for this task, deliberately deferred to a future task: a byte-volume metric (derivable from pg_stat_io's op_bytes on PG16/17 or the direct byte counters on PG18, but still not real disk throughput) and any UI chart/visualization. The earlier requirement asking for an 'autovacuum consumed X MB/s' chart is withdrawn — see the design doc's 'Scope kararı' section for the rationale.

acceptance_criteria.text: docs/autovacuum-cost-diagnosis-design.md written, live-tested on 3 real instances (instance_pk=6/8/23), and consolidated across FOUR review rounds (own live tests plus three independent external reviews; official PostgreSQL 11/13/18 docs fetched live to settle version questions). Final design: Diagnosis 0 (BONUS evidence only, PG16+ gated, never primary — autovacuum-worker vs. client-backend I/O OPERATION counts via fact.pg_io_stat_delta with object='relation', since 15/25 registered instances are below PG16); Diagnosis 2 (primary, all PG versions — IO-wait ratio; proves only that an I/O completion was awaited, NOT that hardware is slow, and independent from Diagnosis 2b); Diagnosis 2b (primary, PG13+ only — the VacuumDelay wait_event was added in PG13 and has always been wait_event_type='Timeout' in every version where it exists; throttle-sleep ratio read alongside effective cost settings); Diagnosis 1 (optional secondary context only, its own >=10 five-minute-bucket gate on BOTH sides — the naive latency window comparison proved unreliable on live data); Diagnosis 3 (code guard: no action text may recommend disabling autovacuum). Wrong claims found and corrected across the rounds: 'VacuumDelay moved Timeout->IO in PG13' (false); the cost_delay 20ms->2ms default drop is PG12, not PG13; the -1 sentinel was NOT introduced in PG12 and never removed (present in PG11's own docs, current through PG17); a high IO-wait ratio does not prove cost_delay is misconfigured; the instance count is 25 not 23 (60% below PG16, not 65%); vacuum_cost_page_hit/miss/dirty are the correct unprefixed names; wait_event IS NULL means 'no wait event reported' not 'actively running'; high VacuumDelay means the cost budget WAS reached (not that the worker couldn't fill it); the '3 test instances all showed X' generalization was wrong (instance_pk=8 sampled 0/0, no signal at all). CLOSED decisions (no longer open): the Diagnosis 2/2b sufficiency gate is count(distinct snapshot_ts) >= 10; runningWorkers is count(distinct pid) at the instance's latest OVERALL activity snapshot (not the latest worker-filtered snapshot, which would misreport 'zero workers now' as a stale historical count); the settings read must use DISTINCT ON + ORDER BY snapshot_ts DESC with a freshness check (the first draft's query returned all historical rows); Diagnosis 0 needs an ordered six-state model (UNKNOWN_CAPABILITY / UNSUPPORTED / INSTANCE_UNREACHABLE / NO_FRESH_DATA / ZERO_IO_WITH_FRESH_DATA / AVAILABLE). Newly discovered in the fourth round: PG18 adds autovacuum_worker_slots which caps effective worker capacity below autovacuum_max_workers (3 PG18 instances in the fleet, parameter not collected at all yet), and ClusterCollector's getDoubleOrZero() silently coerces source NULLs to 0.0, which makes the NO_FRESH_DATA vs. ZERO_IO_WITH_FRESH_DATA distinction impossible without a fix. NO open design decisions remain. The two items the fourth round called open were not design questions: the timestamp type is an implementation test requirement (the decision is already made — normalize both OffsetDateTime and java.sql.Timestamp), and AC3 target selection is a verification procedure (query control.instance_capability at verification time). The fifth round additionally closed four contracts: four independent status fields on the worker record (currentWorkerStatus/ioWaitStatus/throttleStatus/capacityStatus) instead of one enum that cannot represent PG12 (IO available, throttle unsupported) or a 9-snapshot window (ratios insufficient, current worker count still valid); a six-state Diagnosis 0 model backed by source_row_count/per-metric-valid-counts/latest_sample_ts in the query itself, with ZERO_IO_WITH_FRESH_DATA named to avoid implying autovacuum did not run; the typed I/O counter refactor promoted from optional to mandatory prerequisite 10 (Long/BigDecimal counters, nullable Double timings, stats_reset in the same record, skip-delta-on-reset, null-aware DeltaCalculator); and a step-by-step effective-settings chain per parameter whose UNKNOWN outcome suppresses the cost_delay recommendation, and freshness thresholds derived from each source collector cadence (x2 + grace) rather than any hardcoded hour count, since hot-refreshed and nightly-refreshed settings have very different staleness bounds. The fifth round also defined what a NULL metric means: rows present but the metric NULL across them is NOT NO_FRESH_DATA — the record still returns AVAILABLE with that metric carried as null and reported as unmeasured, never as zero.

Implementation per the design doc's 'AC2 implementasyon sırası' section. STEP 0 — land the 10 confirmed prerequisite fixes from the doc's 'Kod önkoşulları' section first; these are foundation bugs the new evidence would otherwise inherit: (1) fetchAutovacuumWorkerStatus() uses count(*) instead of the two-step distinct-pid-at-latest-overall-snapshot definition; (2) findBloatedTables() has no relid, blocking per-table cost-override lookup by (instance_pk, dbid, relid); (3) control.table_relopts_snapshot stores only raw reloptions text, needs a migration adding parsed nullable cost-override columns plus a tested parser; (4) diagnoseBloat()'s evidence text is silently dropped when the message template fails to render; (5) ClusterCollector's previousIoSamples reads stats_reset but never uses it in the delta comparison; (6) the 'autovacuum' on/off parameter is in NEITHER settings list (not just missing from HOT — it's absent from the nightly SETTINGS_QUERY too), needed for the Diagnosis 3 guard; (7) vacuum_cost_delay/vacuum_cost_limit are in the nightly SETTINGS_QUERY but missing from HOT_SETTINGS_QUERY (autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay/limit are already in both — don't confuse them); (8) autovacuum_worker_slots (PG18+, caps effective capacity below autovacuum_max_workers) is not collected at all, and 3 fleet instances are PG18; (9) ClusterCollector's getDoubleOrZero() coerces source NULLs to 0.0 for I/O counters, which makes Diagnosis 0's NO_FRESH_DATA vs. ZERO_IO_WITH_FRESH_DATA distinction impossible — must become NULL-safe or carry a separate flag. Prerequisite 10 (new, mandatory — was previously mislabeled optional): the I/O sample cache must become typed, since prerequisites 5 (stats_reset awareness), 9 (NULL preservation) and the Diagnosis 0 state model all mutate the same structure — Long/BigDecimal counters, nullable Double timings, previous stats_reset held in the same typed record, no delta written on the reset cycle, and a null-aware DeltaCalculator. THEN: fetchAutovacuumWorkerStatus() returns a typed record carrying runningWorkers, maxWorkers, workerSlots, effectiveWorkerCapacity, totalSamples, distinctSnapshots, ioWaitSamples, throttleSleepSamples, noWaitEventSamples, otherWaitSamples, latestSnapshotTs and FOUR INDEPENDENT status fields — currentWorkerStatus, ioWaitStatus, throttleStatus, capacityStatus — because a single enum cannot express PG12 (ioWait AVAILABLE while throttle is UNSUPPORTED_VERSION), a 9-snapshot window (ratios INSUFFICIENT_DATA while the current worker count is still AVAILABLE), or a missing PG18 worker_slots value (capacity UNKNOWN only). The three named wait buckets plus the residual otherWaitSamples sum to totalSamples by definition — assert this identity in a test and assert the residual is never negative. Sufficiency gate is count(distinct snapshot_ts) >= 10 (a closed decision, not an open question). Effective cost settings resolved per parameter independently through an explicit chain: table override >= 0 wins outright; table override == -1 or absent falls through to the global autovacuum_* setting (read via DISTINCT ON + ORDER BY snapshot_ts DESC with a freshness check, since pg_settings_snapshot is a time-series table); global -1 falls through to vacuum_* (PG11+ behavior). Missing, malformed or stale at any step yields UNKNOWN, which SUPPRESSES the cost_delay recommendation entirely. Freshness thresholds derive from each source collector cadence x2 plus grace — never a hardcoded hour count, since hot-refreshed and nightly-refreshed settings have very different staleness bounds. The 'lower cost_delay' recommendation gate is effectiveCostDelay > versionDefault (20ms on PG11, 2ms on PG12+) — NOT merely 'non-default', since 0ms/1ms are non-default but below the default and must not trigger it; and never on IO-wait evidence alone. fetchAutovacuumIoImpact() implements a SIX-state ordered model (UNKNOWN_CAPABILITY / UNSUPPORTED / INSTANCE_UNREACHABLE / NO_FRESH_DATA / ZERO_IO_WITH_FRESH_DATA / AVAILABLE), checking has_pg_stat_io and is_reachable explicitly, deciding NO_FRESH_DATA from source_row_count and latest_sample_ts rather than from counter values, using object='relation' and a client-reads=0 guard against infinite ratios. A metric that is NULL across all returned rows is a distinct case from both of those: the state stays AVAILABLE, the metric is carried as null and worded as unmeasured, and partial NULL coverage sums only the non-null rows while reporting the covered fraction. Zero relation I/O with fresh data must NOT be worded as 'autovacuum did not run' — pages may all have been buffer hits. All generated text stays observational, never causal, and never claims hardware slowness from wait_event_type='IO' (which only proves an I/O completion was awaited). Wire into scenario 3 and 4.5's diagnosis text on the EXISTING dead_tuple_ratio alert (AlertCode.USER_DEFINED_RULE) — not a new alert type, not adaptive alerting. mvn compile && mvn test pass; add the unit tests enumerated at the end of the design doc, including both timestamp types via queryForList() (resolving AC1's one remaining open item) and the autovacuum-disable guard.

Live verification, with target instances selected AT VERIFICATION TIME rather than fixed here — re-query control.instance_capability to pick one current PG16+ instance, one PG13-15 instance, and one PG12 instance, since pg_major values change (instance_pk=23 already moved PG15->PG17 mid-task via a live pg_upgrade, so any hardcoded list here would be stale). Confirm: the new evidence sentences appear correctly in a real triggered dead_tuple_ratio alert message; on the PG16+ instance Diagnosis 0 produces plausible operation counts with the object='relation' filter applied (this filter was added after the original measurement, so re-run and re-record the numbers rather than reusing the pre-filter figures); on the sub-PG16 instance Diagnosis 0 reports an explicit unsupported state while Diagnoses 2/2b still appear; on the PG12 instance Diagnosis 2b reports UNSUPPORTED_VERSION rather than a silent zero while Diagnosis 2 still works; the cost-setting guard suppresses 'lower cost_delay' where the effective setting is at or below the version default; and the six-state Diagnosis 0 model correctly distinguishes a real zero from missing data, and a metric that is NULL across all rows is reported as unmeasured rather than as zero.

WRONG CLAIMS CORRECTED: cost_delay's 20ms->2ms default drop happened in PG12, not PG13 (PG13 kept the PG12 default unchanged); the -1 sentinel ('fall back to vacuum_cost_delay/vacuum_cost_limit') was never removed and is still current behavior through PG17 — both were stated backwards in the original design and are now fixed. Also corrected: a high IO-wait ratio (Diagnosis 2) does NOT prove cost_delay is set too high — IO wait and VacuumDelay are independent wait causes (one is disk latency, the other is deliberate config-driven sleep); the 'lower cost_delay' action must be gated on Diagnosis 2b's throttle evidence, not Diagnosis 2's IO evidence. CODE GAPS CONFIRMED (all now documented as AC2 prerequisites, not the reviewer's guesses — verified against actual line numbers): fetchAutovacuumWorkerStatus() counts count(*) over a 2-minute window instead of distinct pid at the latest snapshot_ts, risking double-counting the same worker across cycles as false 'saturation'; findBloatedTables() doesn't select relid, which blocks any per-table cost-override lookup by (instance_pk, dbid, relid); control.table_relopts_snapshot (V093) only stores raw reloptions text, no parsed cost columns exist yet; diagnoseBloat()'s evidence text is silently dropped if the alert message template fails to render (falls back to a generic message with no diagnosis/action context); ClusterCollector's previousIoSamples cache reads stats_reset but never uses it in the delta comparison, risking a wrong I/O count immediately after a pg_stat_reset_shared('io') call; I/O counters are stored as Double before being cast to long (not a live precision-loss risk at realistic magnitudes, but a type-correctness smell); OffsetDateTime timestamp handling was checked and found consistent (no getTimestamp() usage, no bug there — this one claim did NOT hold up).

[SUPERSEDED IN PART — the fourth round's own summary; the fifth round below closed four contracts it had left underspecified] Fourth review round (2026-08-26): the design doc was consolidated a second time — earlier rounds had appended correction notes beside wrong text instead of replacing it, which itself produced contradictions (Diagnosis 0 described as both primary and PG16+ bonus, instance count given as both 23 and 25, the -1 sentinel described as both introduced-in-PG12 and present-since-PG11). The doc now carries one canonical explanation per topic. This round also fetched three official PostgreSQL doc pages live to settle version questions definitively: PG11 runtime-config-autovacuum confirms the -1 sentinel predates PG12 (so the previous rounds claim that PG12 introduced it was itself wrong); PG13 monitoring-stats confirms VacuumDelay was added in PG13 and sits in the Timeout wait_event_type table (so the correct phrasing is always-Timeout-where-it-exists, not always-Timeout-in-every-version); PG18 runtime-config-autovacuum confirms autovacuum_worker_slots caps effective worker capacity below autovacuum_max_workers and that cost_limit is distributed proportionally among running workers — a parameter pgstat does not collect at all despite 3 PG18 instances in the fleet. A code-audit pass additionally confirmed two new prerequisites: the settings-read query in the design draft returned all historical rows (needs DISTINCT ON + ORDER BY snapshot_ts DESC plus a freshness check, since pg_settings_snapshot is a partitioned time-series table), and ClusterCollector.getDoubleOrZero() silently coerces source NULLs to 0.0 for I/O counters, which makes Diagnosis 0 NO_DATA-vs-real-zero discrimination impossible without a fix. The prerequisite count is now 9 (was miscounted as 5 then 7), and the earlier claim that timestamp handling was verified-clean was correctly reopened — only direct ResultSet paths were checked, not the queryForList() access pattern this task will use. Scope was also narrowed deliberately: the original requirement for an autovacuum consumed X MB/s chart is withdrawn (PostgreSQL exposes operation counts, and byte counters only from PG16 op_bytes / PG18 direct columns, none of which equal real disk throughput) and moved to a future task.

CURRENT (fifth review round, 2026-08-26): a further review found the fourth round had left four technical contracts underspecified enough to block AC2, all now closed in the design doc. (1) A SINGLE status enum on the worker-evidence record is impossible: on PG12 ioWaitStatus is AVAILABLE while throttleStatus must be UNSUPPORTED_VERSION; with only 9 distinct snapshots the ratios are INSUFFICIENT_DATA while currentWorkerStatus can still be AVAILABLE; and a missing PG18 autovacuum_worker_slots value should degrade only capacityStatus. The record now carries four independent status fields (currentWorkerStatus, ioWaitStatus, throttleStatus, capacityStatus) plus workerSlots and effectiveWorkerCapacity. (2) Diagnosis 0 could not actually decide fresh-zero-vs-no-data from its own query: it now also returns source_row_count, per-metric valid counts, and latest_sample_ts, and the state model grew to six ordered states (UNKNOWN_CAPABILITY / UNSUPPORTED / INSTANCE_UNREACHABLE / NO_FRESH_DATA / ZERO_IO_WITH_FRESH_DATA / AVAILABLE) with has_pg_stat_io and is_reachable checked explicitly. The state was renamed ZERO_IO_WITH_FRESH_DATA because zero relation I/O does not mean autovacuum did not run (pages may all have been buffer hits). (3) The Double-to-typed refactor was still marked optional despite three separate prerequisites depending on it; it is now mandatory prerequisite 10, specifying Long/BigDecimal counters, nullable Double timings, previous stats_reset stored in the same typed record, skip-delta-on-reset, and a null-aware DeltaCalculator (also correcting the earlier 52-bit claim: binary64 is exact only to 2^53). (4) The effective-settings chain is now written step-by-step per parameter with an explicit UNKNOWN outcome for missing/malformed/stale values that suppresses the cost_delay recommendation, and freshness thresholds are defined as collector-cadence x2 + grace rather than the previously hardcoded 25 hours (which was far too loose for settings refreshed every 3 hours). Also corrected: the three named wait buckets plus the residual sum to totalSamples BY DEFINITION (the doc had claimed the opposite); Diagnosis 2 opened by saying real disk I/O wait when PostgreSQL only guarantees an I/O completion is being awaited; and PG18 cost balancing has a documented exception that matters directly here — workers processing tables with per-table cost storage parameters are excluded from balancing entirely (verified against PG18 routine-vacuuming docs), which invalidates any per-worker budget arithmetic for exactly the tables this feature reads overrides for.

tasks.title: Collector restart loses one collection cycle per table/statement due to in-memory prev-value caches
tasks.problem: While live-verifying PGSTAT-P0-034's VACUUM-resolve fix, discovered that DbObjectsCollector.previousTableStats (a ConcurrentHashMap<String, Map<String,Long>> instance field) is empty right after any collector restart/deploy — its baseline-detection logic (`if (prev == null) continue;`) then treats the FIRST post-restart collection cycle for every table as a fresh baseline and writes zero rows to fact.pg_table_stat_delta, silently skipping that cycle. Confirmed live: a deploy at 12:14:56+03 meant the 12:24:25 collection cycle for instance_pk=26/dbid=62751 produced last_db_objects_collect_at movement but zero fact.pg_table_stat_delta rows; the next cycle (12:39:25) resumed normally. Same in-memory-cache pattern likely exists in StatementsCollector (previousSamples) and possibly other collectors — not confirmed for all of them yet. Impact is a one-cycle (~15-30 min, depending on schedule_profile) gap in delta data per table/statement per restart, not data loss beyond that cycle, and not alert-incorrectness (the hasRecentData guard from PGSTAT-P0-034 already prevents this gap from causing a false auto-resolve).
requirements: Survey every collector with an in-memory prev-value cache (DbObjectsCollector confirmed; check StatementsCollector, ClusterCollector, and any others using a similar baseline-on-null-previous pattern).

Design a cross-collector-consistent way to persist the last raw (not delta) cumulative values so a restart can rehydrate the cache instead of starting from an empty baseline — likely a new small control/ops table keyed by (instance_pk, collector, entity_key) storing the raw counters as of the last successful cycle.
Must not change the existing delta semantics (negative delta still means reset/wraparound and is skipped) — this only affects the FIRST post-restart cycle's baseline detection, not ongoing behavior.
Given the blast radius (touches every collector's core loop), this needs its own design pass before implementation — do not bolt a one-off fix onto a single collector.

acceptance_criteria.text: A written design (schema + which collectors are affected + rehydration logic) is reviewed and approved before any code changes.
Implementation covers at least DbObjectsCollector and StatementsCollector; mvn compile && mvn test pass.

Live verification: after a deploy/restart, the first post-restart collection cycle for a previously-tracked table/statement produces a normal delta row (not silently skipped) — confirmed via fact.pg_table_stat_delta / fact.pgss_delta sample_ts continuity across a restart.

implementation_plan: Not yet designed — this is a placeholder pending a dedicated design pass (see next_action). Survey step: grep every collector for a bare instance-field Map used as a prev-sample cache (DbObjectsCollector.previousTableStats confirmed; StatementsCollector.previousSamples and ClusterCollector are suspects, not yet confirmed).
verification_plan: Live: trigger a deploy, immediately compare pre- and post-restart sample_ts rows in the relevant fact tables for a known tracked entity, confirm no gap.
verification_evidence: Discovered and root-caused live on 2026-08-24 while verifying PGSTAT-P0-034's VACUUM-resolve fix: docker inspect confirmed collector restart at 12:14:56+03; control.database_state showed last_db_objects_collect_at advancing to 12:24:25 for the affected instance/database with zero corresponding fact.pg_table_stat_delta rows; the next cycle (12:39:25) resumed normally with a correct delta reflecting the customer's VACUUM FULL. Code read of DbObjectsCollector.java confirmed the root cause: `Map<String, Long> prev = previousTableStats.put(cacheKey, current); if (prev == null) continue;` — an in-memory-only cache with no persistence across restarts.

Deliberately deferred implementation: the customer asked for 'the logical and healthy' fix, which was assessed as a persisted raw-counter rehydration mechanism — but that touches every collector's core loop and needed its own design pass rather than a same-session bolt-on fix to a single collector.
tasks.next_action: Schedule a dedicated design session: survey all collectors for the same in-memory-cache-on-restart pattern, design the persisted raw-state table and rehydration logic, then implement and verify before closing.

tasks.title: Partition drop threshold counts retention policies no active instance uses, so partitions live far past their retention
tasks.problem: PurgeEvaluator computed every partition-drop cutoff as max(retention) over control.retention_policy filtered only by p.is_active and p.purge_enabled — it never joined control.instance_inventory, so a policy that exists but is assigned to no active instance still widened the window. In production on 2026-08-27 that meant r12-long (30 days, 0 active instances) set the cutoff instead of r6-default (14 days, 1 instance) / r3-short (7 days, 24 instances): raw delta partitions were kept 30 days instead of 14. The wasted-space consequence is worse than the extra partitions: instance-scoped batched DELETE still ran on those retained partitions, so 24 of 25 instances had their rows deleted while the partition itself stayed. Because a past day partition is never written again, the pages autovacuum freed were marked reusable but never reused and never returned to the OS. pgstattuple measured ~30-45% free space in pgss_delta partitions (289-296 MB each) and roughly 3 GB total across the delta families, with n_dead_tup = 0 — invisible to any dead-tuple based check. The customer had been reclaiming this by hand with periodic VACUUM FULL, which took an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock and refilled within days.
requirements: Every partition-drop cutoff must be derived only from retention policies that at least one active instance actually references, so an unused policy cannot widen the retention window.
Retention policies must remain defined and active even when unused — the customer keeps r12-long available to assign later, so the fix must not require deleting or deactivating policy rows.
The fix must cover all six cutoff computations in PurgeEvaluator (raw delta, snapshot, table freeze, nightly snapshot, hourly agg, daily agg), not just the raw delta path where it was first observed.

The snapshot path converts hours to days; its existing 1-day safety margin must be preserved exactly, since day-granularity partitions must not be dropped while part of the retention window still falls inside them.

acceptance_criteria.text: PurgeEvaluator has a single longestUsedRetentionCutoff(String retentionExpr) helper that joins control.instance_inventory to control.retention_policy and filters on i.is_active and p.is_active and p.purge_enabled, and all six cutoff sites call it — no remaining query selects from control.retention_policy without the instance join.

The snapshot cutoff keeps its original arithmetic: max(ceil(hours/24) - 1) is equivalent to the previous ceil(max(hours)/24) - 1 because ceil is monotonic, so the drop boundary is unchanged apart from which policies are considered.
mvn compile and mvn test pass (52/52).

Live verification after deploy: the raw delta cutoff moves from 2026-07-28 to 2026-08-13, the nightly purge drops the partitions older than the new cutoff, and total database size falls by roughly 10 GB without any manual VACUUM FULL.
Customer confirms that periodic manual VACUUM FULL is no longer needed to keep the database size stable.

implementation_plan: collector/src/main/java/com/pgstat/collector/service/PurgeEvaluator.java: add private LocalDate longestUsedRetentionCutoff(String retentionExpr) in the helper section, documenting the production measurement that motivated it.

Replace the six inline jdbc.queryForObject cutoff queries (purgeRawDeltaFacts, purgeSnapshotFacts, purgeTableFreezeFacts, purgeNightlySnapshotFacts, purgeHourlyAgg, purgeDailyAgg) with calls to the helper, passing each one its own retention expression.

Diagnosis chain: partition inventory showed en_eski = 20260728 (30 days) across six delta families totalling 21.7 GB; control.retention_policy showed r12-long = 30 days with kullanan_aktif_instance = 0 while 24 instances used r3-short (7) and 1 used r6-default (14); pgstattuple on the retained partitions showed dead_tuple_percent 0.0 with free_space 289-296 MB per pgss_delta partition, confirming the space was freed-but-unreturned pages rather than dead tuples.

Ruled out first: purge row deletion was working (n_tup_del 650-720k per partition, partitions older than 14 days held only 4 MB total), autovacuum was healthy (last_autovacuum current on every large table, n_dead_tup 0), and there was no bloat in the dead-tuple sense — which is why no existing alert caught it.

tasks.title: Bloat suppression froze an already-open alert and never fired on tables whose dead tuples stopped growing
tasks.problem: The transient-bloat suppression added on 2026-08-27 (PGSTAT-P1-011 follow-up) had two defects that surfaced together in production on the same day. First, control.bloat_scenario_streak only advanced when the dead-tuple count was strictly greater than the previous reading, so a table that had already bottomed out stayed invisible forever: security.user on instance 2 sat at 6 live / 3224 dead, never vacuumed, reporting the same count every evaluation, so the streak reset to 1 each time and the alert threshold was never reached. Second, the suppression branch called updateLastEval with the computed severity and then continued without touching ops.alert. That wrote last_alert_at = now() (falsely arming the 60-minute cooldown) and left current_severity populated (making the next cycle resolve condition misleading), while an alert opened before suppression existed was left frozen: alert 112959 stayed open with a message from 2026-08-21 naming public.t_currency_rate_active, a table the customer had already vacuumed, while five other tables on the same instance were above threshold and last_seen_at had not moved for over two hours.
requirements: The persistence counter must measure how long the scenario has persisted, not whether dead tuples keep climbing, so a table that stopped growing while still un-vacuumed is not silently ignored.

Transient accumulations must still be suppressed — they are handled by the counter row being deleted once the table stops exceeding the threshold or moves to another scenario, not by resetting on a flat reading.
Suppression must not write a severity into control.alert_rule_last_eval, since a suppressed evaluation means no alert is being raised.
Suppression must not leave an already-open alert untouched; if the situation is not worth alerting on, an open alert is resolved rather than frozen with a stale message.

acceptance_criteria.text: bumpScenarioStreak advances the counter on every evaluation and resets to 1 only when the dead-tuple count strictly falls; the rule is mirrored in a pure static shouldResetStreak(previous, current) that the SQL case expression matches.
The suppression branch calls updateLastEval with a null severity and, when a previous severity exists and auto_resolve is on, resolves the open alert before continuing.
Four unit tests cover the counter rule: flat count advances, growing count advances, falling count resets, unknown previous count advances. mvn compile and mvn test pass (56/56).

tasks.title: Granular threshold alerts collapse every offending table into one instance-level alert, so only the worst one is ever visible
tasks.problem: evaluateThresholdPerRecord builds a single alert per rule and instance (alert_key = rule:{ruleId}:instance:{instancePk}) and renders only exceeding.get(0), the worst record. Every other table over the threshold is invisible: it never appears in a message, never gets its own lifecycle, and never enters control.bloat_scenario_streak, which is keyed per table. The customer hit this directly on 2026-08-27: five tables on instance 2 were over the dead-tuple threshold (security.user 99.81%, t_content_update 98.04%, t_ext_hotel_product 94.80%, t_ext_hotel_payment_types 94.25%, t_supplier_rez 93.60%), all never vacuumed, but only one was named. After fixing the table the alert named, the next worst simply took its place, so the operator has to fix one, wait a cycle, and discover the next - with no way to see the real size of the problem. The customer called the behaviour nonsensical and asked for it to be fixed. The same collapse applies to statement_metric and index_metric, which share this code path.
requirements: Each record over the threshold must get its own alert with its own key, so it opens, updates and resolves independently of the others.

Notifications must not fan out one-per-alert: the delivery layer sends a single summary message per rule and instance per evaluation listing the affected records, so five broken tables do not mean five Telegram messages.
Existing open instance-level alerts from the old key format must be resolved by a migration with a superseded note, so the two formats never coexist confusingly.
The per-table persistence counter (control.bloat_scenario_streak) must now be consulted for every exceeding record, not only the worst one - that is the point of splitting the alerts.

Alert volume must stay bounded in the pathological case: a newly onboarded instance where dozens of tables are simultaneously over threshold must not open an unbounded number of alerts in one evaluation. Decide and document the cap and what happens to records beyond it.

acceptance_criteria.text: alert_key for granular threshold alerts identifies the record, not just the instance (for table_metric: rule, instance, dbid and relid), so each offending table has an independent alert row in ops.alert.
Every record over the threshold is evaluated - diagnosis, suppression and streak counter all run per record - instead of only exceeding.get(0).
Notification delivery batches per rule and instance per evaluation: opening five table alerts produces five ops.alert rows but a single outbound summary message naming the affected tables.
A migration resolves open alerts whose alert_key matches the old instance-level format for granular rules, recording a superseded reason.
A documented cap bounds how many per-record alerts one evaluation may open, with the overflow surfaced rather than silently dropped.
mvn compile and mvn test pass, with unit coverage for the new key construction and the batching decision.
Live verification on instance 2: all five currently offending tables appear as separate alerts, fixing one resolves only that alert, and the batch notification lists them together.

implementation_plan: AlertRuleEvaluator.evaluateThresholdPerRecord: replace the single-record path with a loop over exceeding, building a per-record alert key and running diagnosis/suppression/streak for each; keep the instance-level key only for non-granular metric types.

Resolve handling: records that dropped below threshold since the last evaluation must have their per-record alerts resolved - compare the current exceeding set against currently open alerts for this rule and instance.
